newsitem.title: PERU: Peru prays for Christmas miracle to free hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peru prays for Christmas miracle to free hostages.

text.p: Marxist rebels fell silent on Tuesday on the fate of an estimated 140 hostages they were holding as Peru prayed for a Christmas miracle to set the captives free.

No communication has come from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers since President Alberto Fujimori sent them a stern message on Saturday telling them to surrender and release all their prisoners.

The captives, mostly top Peruvian government officials, Japanese businessmen or ambassadors to Peru, faced a nightmare Christmas under the guns of the rebels in foul, unsanitary conditions without water or electricity.

Red Cross workers brought Italian-style cake -- traditional in many Latin American nations at Christmas -- for the captives in the Japanese ambassador's residence while reporters outside added a seasonal touch by decorating their equipment with Christmas lights and putting up a small plastic tree.

Plunged into gloom by the crisis, Peruvians prepared for a miserable Yuletide. One local bishop, Miguel Irizar, urged his countrymen not to celebrate at all. "We cannot have parties or be frivolous," he said.

Local television played specially composed songs and messages for the captives, but the lack of electricity inside the besieged residence meant it was unlikely the hostages would hear them. Overnight, a small group of Roman Catholic Peruvians held a candlelit vigil nearby.
"The solidarity has been shown in many ways and now more than ever we pray to the Virgin Mary to soften the hearts of the captors and let all the hostages out," one participant said.
Relatives wrote seasonal messages to their loved ones on special forms, not knowing how long it would be until they were reunited.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, whose government has most at stake in the affair after Peru's because of the large number of Japanese hostages, predicted on Tuesday that the crisis would be a long, drawn-out affair. Lima would try to wear the guerrillas down rather than flush them out by force, he said.

"I think it will take time to resolve the crisis," Hashimoto told reporters shortly after speaking by telephone to Fujimori, a Peruvian whose parents came from Japan. "The fact that it will take time means that no get-tough approach will be taken."
Fujimori's government believes the ball is now firmly in the court of the 20 or so rebels and wants them to give a response to its proposals before making any move, Peruvian media reported.

The government has given no official information to the hordes of waiting world media since the crisis began but rumours have swirled thick and fast. One story going the rounds among diplomats in Lima was that the government might be secretly negotiating a safe passage to Cuba for the rebels in exchange for the release of all the hostages.

A diplomat at the Cuban Embassy told Reuters Havana's ambassador here, Pedro Diaz, had conferred with Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina on Monday but declined to go into details. Diaz, who spent five days as a captive in the residence before being released with a group of 225 hostages on Sunday night, was away from the embassy in meetings on Tuesday, the diplomat added.
In Hamburg, Germany, a man claiming to be the MRTA's international spokesman said the rebels would never surrender.

"Effectively, what the government of President Fujimori is asking is that the group ... gives up," Isaac Velazco told the Cable News Network. "The word surrender or capitulation is not in the vocabulary of the Tupac Amaru soldier."

A Peruvian commando team was standing by to storm the residence as a last resort. But Fujimori has told the rebels he would not use force and would consider a peaceful "way out" if they laid down their arms and gave up all their hostages.
His plea, and later ones from U.S. President Bill Clinton and Pope John Paul II to release the captives, seem to have fallen on deaf ears.

The MRTA fighters seized the residence a week ago during a posh reception to commemorate Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday, taking more than 500 hostages. Many -- including all the American, British and German captives -- have been freed.
